stem: If one of the 18th-century fragments is selected at random, what is the probability that it is made of linen?
stimulus:
A museum of textile history catalogued its collection of woven fragments by fiber and by the century in which each fragment was made. The results are shown in the table.

Woven Fragments by Fiber and Century
Fiber | 17th century | 18th century | Total
Wool | 24 | 36 | 60
Linen | 16 | 44 | 60
Total | 40 | 80 | 120
explanation: The condition is "one of the 18th-century fragments," so the 18th-century column is now your whole world. Its total, 80, is the denominator. The linen cell in that column is 44. The probability is $\frac{44}{80} = \frac{11}{20}$.

A.why: You divided the 44 linen 18th-century fragments by the grand total, 120. That gives the probability that a fragment from the whole collection is both linen and from the 18th century, not the probability among the 18th-century fragments only.

B.why: You used the right column but took the wool cell, $\frac{36}{80} = \frac{9}{20}$. That is the probability of wool, not linen.

D.why: You swapped the condition and the target and divided 44 by the linen total, 60. That answers "of the linen fragments, what fraction are from the 18th century?", which is a different question.

explanation: The condition is "one of the deep wells," so keep only the Deep row. Its total, 60, is the denominator. The deep wells above the limit number 6. The probability is $\frac{6}{60} = \frac{1}{10}$.

A.why: You divided 6 by the grand total, 120. That is the probability that a well chosen from all 120 is both deep and above the limit, not the probability among deep wells only.

C.why: You swapped the condition and the target and divided 6 by 24, the total of wells above the limit. That answers "of the wells above the limit, what fraction are deep?"

D.why: You used the Deep row but took the below-limit cell, $\frac{54}{60} = \frac{9}{10}$. That is the probability of the opposite outcome.
